title: Depreciation
tagline: Why assets lose value, how the straight line and written down value methods measure it, and how each is recorded in the accounts.

overview.intro: A delivery van bought for ₹6,00,000 will not be worth ₹6,00,000 at the end of the year. It has been used, it wears out, and its market value falls. Charging that fall against the years that benefited from the asset is the purpose of depreciation. Without it, the profit of the year of purchase is understated and the profits of later years are overstated, because the cost of the asset is being treated as though it were consumed all at once. This unit covers the meaning and need for depreciation, its causes, the two methods prescribed for the course, the entries that record them, and the disposal of an asset at the end of its working life.

facts.label: Straight line method
facts.value: Depreciation = (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life; the same amount every year.

facts.label: Written down value method
facts.value: Depreciation = rate × book value at the start of the year, so the charge falls each year.

facts.label: Journal entry
facts.value: Depreciation a/c Dr, to Asset a/c (or to provision for depreciation); profit and loss a/c Dr, to Depreciation a/c.

facts.label: Exam weight
facts.value: A depreciation account or asset-account problem appears every year alongside a theory question on causes.

learningOutcomes: Define depreciation and state its need and causes.
Calculate annual depreciation under the straight line and written down value methods.
Record depreciation in the accounts and allocate it to the profit and loss account.
Prepare an asset account showing acquisition, depreciation and disposal.
Compare the two methods and identify when each is appropriate.

learn.title: Meaning, need, causes and objectives of depreciation

blocks.text: Depreciation is the permanent and continuous decrease in the value of a fixed asset arising from wear and tear, the passage of time, or obsolescence. It is a non-cash expense: the business pays for the asset when it buys it, and depreciation simply spreads that cost across the years the asset serves. Its need follows from the matching convention. A machine bought in April helps produce revenue for the next six years, so its cost must be charged against those six years’ profits rather than against the first April alone. Depreciation also helps the business set aside funds for replacement by showing a truer profit, and it is required so that the balance sheet does not overstate assets.

items: Wear and tear from use: the most common cause for machinery and vehicles.
Passage of time: buildings and leases decline simply because years elapse.
Obsolescence: a new machine makes the old one uneconomic before it is worn out.
Market changes: demand for a particular model falls and its realisable value drops.
Efflux of time: for assets like patents or leases with a fixed legal life.
Depletion: for wasting assets such as mines or quarries where the resource itself is consumed.

blocks.caption: Objectives that depreciation serves
rows: Matches the cost of the asset to the revenue it helped earn
Shows assets at a value that reflects their remaining usefulness
Retains profit in the business that can buy a successor asset
Charges the same cost to every period the asset served
Required by accounting standards and by the companies act for listed firms

items.text: A machine costing ₹4,50,000 with a residual value of ₹50,000 and a five-year life loses ₹80,000 a year under the straight line method.
items.note: The depreciable amount of ₹4,00,000 is spread evenly across the five years of service.

items.text: A van is sold after three years for more than its written down value.
items.note: The excess is a profit on disposal credited to the profit and loss account in the year of sale.

blocks.text: The straight line method, also called the fixed instalment method, charges the same amount of depreciation every year of the asset’s life. The depreciable amount is the cost of the asset less its estimated residual or scrap value, and this is divided by the number of years of useful life. If a machine costs ₹5,20,000, is expected to be sold for ₹20,000 after eight years, the annual charge is (5,20,000 − 20,000) ÷ 8 = ₹62,500. The method is simple, uniform and easy to apply when the asset gives a steady service each year.

blocks.caption: Straight line charge on a machine costing ₹5,20,000, residual ₹20,000, life 8 years

items: Suitable when the asset is expected to give uniform service throughout its life.
Simple to compute and easy to understand for a reader of the accounts.
Charge per year remains constant, which makes budgeting straightforward.
Not suitable for assets whose repair costs rise sharply in later years.
The depreciation rate is expressed on cost, so the percentage never changes.

items.text: Furniture costing ₹1,60,000 with a scrap value of ₹20,000 and a six-year life: (1,60,000 − 20,000) ÷ 6 = ₹23,333 per year.
items.note: The same ₹23,333 is charged in each of the six years regardless of how the furniture is used.

items.text: A motor car costing ₹9,00,000 is depreciated at 20% on cost with a residual value of ₹1,00,000.
items.note: Twenty per cent of cost is ₹1,80,000 a year, so the asset reaches its residual value in four years and four months of charge.

blocks.text: The written down value method, also called the reducing balance method, charges depreciation at a fixed percentage on the book value of the asset at the beginning of each year. The book value is cost less accumulated depreciation, so the charge itself falls year after year. A machine costing ₹1,00,000 depreciated at 20% loses ₹20,000 in the first year, leaving a book value of ₹80,000; the second year’s charge is 20% of ₹80,000, that is ₹16,000, leaving ₹64,000. The method matches the higher repair costs of old assets against a smaller depreciation charge, keeping the total annual burden roughly level.

blocks.caption: Written down value charge at 20% on a machine costing ₹1,00,000

items: The charge is a fixed percentage of the opening book value, not of the original cost.
The amount of depreciation reduces every year as the book value falls.
Well suited to assets that are expensive to maintain as they age.
Uses a higher rate than the straight line method because the base shrinks.
Assets never depreciate to zero under this method, so a residual value is implicit.

items.text: A tool costing ₹50,000 is depreciated at 30% on written down value. Year one charge is ₹15,000, leaving ₹35,000; year two charge is ₹10,500.
items.note: The rate stays at 30% while the rupee charge falls, which is the defining feature of the method.

items.text: Compare 20% on cost with 25% on written down value for a ₹2,00,000 asset.
items.note: On cost the charge is a constant ₹40,000; on written down value it starts at ₹50,000 and falls to ₹37,500 in year two.

learn.title: Recording depreciation and disposing of an asset

blocks.text: Depreciation is recorded by transferring the charge from the asset to the profit and loss account. Under the straight line method the entry is Depreciation account debit and Asset account credit, with the total then closed to the profit and loss account by debiting profit and loss and crediting depreciation. Under the written down value method, where the asset account is deliberately left at cost, a provision for depreciation account is maintained instead: depreciation debits the provision account and credits the provision itself, and the provision is shown in the balance sheet as a deduction from the asset.

blocks.caption: Journal entries for depreciation and disposal
rows: Depreciation a/c Dr, to Asset a/c
Profit and loss a/c Dr, to Depreciation a/c
Charge debited against the year’s profit
Cash a/c Dr, Provision for dep. a/c Dr, Loss on sale a/c Dr, to Asset a/c
Asset removed, loss charged to profit and loss
Cash a/c Dr, Provision for dep. a/c Dr, to Asset a/c, to Profit on sale a/c
Excess of cash over book value is a gain

blocks.text: At disposal the asset account must be cleared. The book value at the date of sale is cost less depreciation to date. Comparing the sale proceeds with that book value gives a profit or a loss, and both are transferred to the profit and loss account of the year of sale. Where the asset was sold in the middle of the year, depreciation is charged up to the date of sale first.

items.text: A machine bought for ₹3,00,000 with ₹1,20,000 depreciation accumulated is sold for ₹1,50,000.
items.note: Book value is ₹1,80,000, so selling at ₹1,50,000 gives a loss of ₹30,000 debited to the profit and loss account.
Proceeds exceed book value by ₹20,000, which is a profit on disposal credited to profit and loss.

blocks.text: Neither method is inherently correct; each is chosen according to the pattern of benefit the asset gives. The straight line method is preferable where the asset’s service is even, such as a building or a lease, and where simplicity matters for statutory reporting. The written down value method is preferable for machinery and vehicles whose repair bills grow with age, because it keeps the combined burden of depreciation and repairs roughly constant. Tax rules in several jurisdictions favour the written down value method, which is why many firms use it for their statutory books and the straight line method for internal reporting.

blocks.caption: Comparison of straight line and written down value methods
rows: Assets with even service: buildings, leases
Assets with rising repairs: machinery, vehicles

items: Charge depreciation to the date of sale before computing any profit or loss on disposal.
Keep the asset at cost and use a provision account when the written down value method is applied.
The method chosen should be applied consistently from year to year.
A change of method is disclosed and justified because it alters reported profit.
Depreciation is an expense in the profit and loss account and never a deduction from capital.

keyPoints: Depreciation is the permanent, continuous fall in the value of a fixed asset.
It is a non-cash expense that matches the asset’s cost against the revenue it helped earn.
Causes: wear and tear, passage of time, obsolescence, market change, efflux of time and depletion.
Straight line charge = (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life.
Written down value charge = rate × opening book value of the year.
The straight line method gives a constant charge and ends exactly at residual value.
The written down value method gives a falling charge and suits assets with rising repair costs.
Depreciation entry: Depreciation a/c Dr, to Asset or to Provision for depreciation.
Profit or loss on disposal = sale proceeds less book value at the date of sale.
The method applied must be consistent, and any change is disclosed.
examFocus: In calculation questions, state the depreciable amount and the divisor before the answer; marks are given for method as well as the figure.
Asset account questions must show the opening balance, additions, depreciation and the disposal entry on the correct sides.
Always compute depreciation up to the date of sale before finding profit or loss, a step examiners look for explicitly.

vocabulary.meaning: Permanent reduction in the value of a fixed asset due to use, time or obsolescence.
Estimated amount realisable when the asset is retired from service.
Cost less depreciation accumulated so far; the base for the reducing balance method.
Loss of value because a newer asset makes the old one uneconomic.
Account accumulating the total depreciation charged against an asset kept at cost.
Decline of an asset that has a fixed legal life, such as a lease or a patent.
Charging costs against the revenue period they help to earn.

options: A cash outflow occurring every year
A non-cash expense spreading the cost of an asset
A reduction in the value of current assets
An addition to the asset in the balance sheet
questions.answer: A non-cash expense spreading the cost of an asset
questions.explanation: The business paid for the asset when it bought it; depreciation only allocates that cost across the years of service.

questions.prompt: A machine costing ₹4,80,000 with a scrap value of ₹30,000 is depreciated over six years under the straight line method. The annual charge is:
Under the written down value method the depreciation charged in year two is calculated on:
options: The original cost of the asset
The book value at the beginning of year two
The average book value over both years
The scrap value of the asset
questions.answer: The book value at the beginning of year two
questions.explanation: A fixed rate is applied to the opening book value of each year, so the base reduces and the charge falls.

questions.prompt: An asset with a book value of ₹1,80,000 is sold for ₹2,10,000. The accounting treatment is:
options: A loss of ₹30,000 debited to profit and loss
A profit of ₹30,000 credited to profit and loss
A gain credited to the capital account directly
No entry until the year end
questions.answer: A profit of ₹30,000 credited to profit and loss
questions.explanation: Proceeds exceed book value by ₹30,000, so a profit on disposal is credited to the profit and loss account of the year of sale.

questions.prompt: The amount expected to be realised when an asset is retired from service is called its __________ value.
questions.explanation: Residual, scrap and salvage value are the estimated proceeds at the end of useful life and are deducted before computing depreciation.

questions.prompt: The method in which the depreciation charge reduces every year because a fixed rate is applied to the reducing balance is the written down __________ method.
questions.explanation: The base is the written down value, that is cost less accumulated depreciation, so the charge shrinks annually.

questions.answer: Four causes are wear and tear from using the asset, the passage of time which reduces the value of buildings and leases, obsolescence where a newer asset makes the existing one uneconomic, and depletion of wasting assets such as mines where the reserve itself is consumed.
questions.explanation: Each cause must be named and briefly explained; listing two causes with explanation earns half marks.

questions.prompt: Give two differences between the straight line and written down value methods.
questions.answer: First, the base: the straight line method charges a fixed amount on cost less residual value while the written down value method charges a fixed percentage on the opening book value. Second, the pattern: the straight line charge is identical every year and ends at the residual value, whereas the written down value charge falls each year and never reduces the asset to zero.
questions.explanation: Both differences must be contrasted; describing only one method earns no marks for comparison.

questions.prompt: A vehicle costing ₹6,00,000 is depreciated at 20% on written down value. Show the depreciation for four years and the book value at the end.
questions.answer: Year one: 20% of ₹6,00,000 = ₹1,20,000, closing book value ₹4,80,000. Year two: 20% of ₹4,80,000 = ₹96,000, closing book value ₹3,84,000. Year three: 20% of ₹3,84,000 = ₹76,800, closing book value ₹3,07,200. Year four: 20% of ₹3,07,200 = ₹61,440, closing book value ₹2,45,760. The total charged over four years is ₹3,54,240.
questions.explanation: Each year must apply the rate to the opening balance of that year rather than to cost; the compounding of the reducing base is the skill being tested.

questions.prompt: A machine costing ₹3,60,000 is depreciated at 25% on written down value. After two years it is sold for ₹1,80,000. Calculate the profit or loss on sale and show the disposal entries.
questions.answer: Year one depreciation is 25% of ₹3,60,000 = ₹90,000, leaving ₹2,70,000. Year two depreciation is 25% of ₹2,70,000 = ₹67,500, so the book value at sale is ₹2,02,500. Selling for ₹1,80,000 gives a loss of ₹22,500. The entries are: Depreciation a/c Dr 67,500 to Provision for depreciation a/c 67,500 for the second year, then Bank a/c Dr 1,80,000, Provision for depreciation a/c Dr 1,57,500 and Loss on sale a/c Dr 22,500 to Machine a/c 3,60,000.
questions.explanation: The chain has three parts: reduce the book value correctly over two years, compare it with proceeds, then clear both the asset and the accumulated provision so no residual balance remains.
